analysis.one_liner: Requires federal permit applicants to get state certification that projects won't degrade state water quality.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on October 11, 1990 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have tightened a section of the Clean Water Act that lets states review federally licensed projects like dams and pipelines. Under it, any applicant for a federal license whose activity might degrade water quality or harm uses a state has designated for its waters — fishing, drinking, recreation — would need the state to certify that the project would not cause that harm. It shifted some power over federally approved projects from Washington to the states where the water is.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states whose waters host federally licensed projects — people who swim, fish, and draw drinking water downstream of dams, pipelines, and other permitted facilities — would gain a stronger state check on projects that could pollute or degrade those waters. State governments would gain leverage over federal licensing decisions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: State residents who use public waters

how_it_helps.text: Expands the Clean Water Act's state certification requirement beyond discharges: any federally licensed or permitted activity that may degrade water quality or impair uses a state has recognized in law — not just activities that discharge pollutants — would need the affected state's certification.

Requires applicants to obtain a state certification that the project will 'achieve, maintain, and protect' the water quality and designated uses in the state's water quality standards, a stronger showing than simply complying with federal discharge rules.

By making state certification a condition for federal licenses and permits, the bill would have given states — the governments closest to the affected rivers and lakes — a meaningful gate over dams, pipelines, and other federally approved projects built in or affecting their waters.

analysis.who_pays: Companies seeking federal licenses or permits — such as hydropower dam operators, pipeline builders, and facilities that discharge into navigable waters — would bear the cost of obtaining state certifications and face the risk that a state denies or conditions approval on water quality grounds, potentially delaying or blocking projects.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federally permitted dam, pipeline, and facility operators

drawbacks.text: The bill would hand states a broader de facto veto over federally licensed projects; states could use certification to delay or block dams, pipelines, and other infrastructure whose benefits extend beyond the state's borders, and federal licensing agencies would have less final say.

The stricter certification standard applies to any activity that 'may' degrade water quality, which gives applicants uncertainty: a project could be denied over potential, not proven, harm, raising costs that get passed to customers and ratepayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — cleaner lakes and rivers and a stronger voice for the states and communities that use them — is real but modest in scope, and the cost is borne by a narrow set of permit applicants and potentially their customers. The main honest objection is the added uncertainty and delay for federally licensed infrastructure. The bill was narrow and never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the final weeks of the Congress, referred to the Senate environment committee, and quietly expired there in January 1991 with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Senator Jeffords introduced the bill on October 11, 1990, in the closing weeks of the 101st Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded — and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies and project developers that need federal licenses or permits are better off, because they never faced the stricter state certification requirement; everyone who would have gained from stronger state oversight of water quality gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. James Jeffords
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican senator sponsored the bill and no one else — of either party — cosponsored it, so no partisan pattern ever took shape.

industries.industry: Hydropower dam operators and other federal license holders
industries.note: Clean Water Act Section 401 certification is the main tool states use to condition or block federally licensed projects like dams; the bill would have widened it from discharges to any activity that could degrade water quality, giving states more power to deny or condition permits. That is a direct cost to permit-dependent project owners and a gain for the communities downstream.

industries.industry: Oil and gas pipeline and infrastructure developers
industries.note: These developers rely on federal permits and would have faced a tougher, broader state certification hurdle covering any potential degradation of state-designated water uses, adding delay and denial risk to projects.

States would gain authority to require proof that federally licensed projects protect the water quality and designated uses in their own standards, strengthening their hand against federal agencies and out-of-state project owners.
